doc.title: Fred Lipsius interviewed by Monk Rowe. Boston, Massachusetts, July 25, 2018

title: Seeing Louis Armstrong on TV and explaining jazz form
summary: Coltrane fingering exercise, then at about seven seeing Satchmo on TV and explaining 32-bar form, choruses and reharmonizing.

story.theme_name: Working with and around Louis Armstrong
story.community_name: Playing with and around Louis Armstrong

blocks.x: On Coltrane I heard he used to play at hotels, and I tell a couple of students, just fingering for an hour before 9:00 or whatever. So I say this is a real test because you can’t cheat yourself. If you play a C sharp major scale, or any scale [scats] really fast, you can just think of “Jada” and play it on your horn and some notes come out quicker than the others, so it really focuses you. It’s a great thing. I only did it once or twice. The other thing I wanted to say about growing up, the influence, besides naturally loving music in my heart, not knowing, it was just there, when I was about seven I saw Satchmo, Louis Armstrong, playing with his group on TV, in black & white TV when TV was new.
You had about two channels, right?

If that. I mean it was five-four-three-two — the channel comes on. But I heard them playing and I don’t remember the feeling I just remember seeing it and I said, “Mom, I want to do that.” I didn’t even know it was jazz. And I’ve told people that don’t know anything about jazz you know, if I’m playing at a concert — well I don’t want to be a teacher too much — but if I mention that I thought everybody was improvising and at a certain point they are but traditional jazz is you play a melody first, and there’s a chord progression, a sequence of chords that follow a progression. And it might be 32 bars or whatever, which is a traditional A-A-B-A form. Eight bars, eight bars, eight bars, eight bars, the bridge being bridging material, or different material. And then you want to hear the last section again, like the A section, like “Over the Rainbow.” [scats] You want to hear it again because it’s so beautiful. The bridge is different. So I tell people when Louis © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

Armstrong and traditional jazz players like Charlie Parker, myself, and all those players, not the out players, they would follow the form of the tune. So they play the melody first or stay close to the melody, and then they would improvise. Whoever was improvising first, the trombone or the piano, and they’d play one chorus which is the whole tune, the form of the tune, 32 bars. And someone would say, “Okay trumpet, two choruses.” So you’d play twice through the whole form. It might take two minutes or whatever. But you play chord by chord the original sequence of the tune’s form. The other thing is with the 32 bars, I do this a lot, I re-harmonize. I change the chords. A lot of jazz composers or arrangers do that because they want to be creative. I love “Over the Rainbow” the way it is, one of the greatest tunes. But I have my own re-harm for it that I’ve never heard anybody do. It’s not about being different it’s about doing what you feel works and opens your heart.
